projects.name: Venvy
projects.one: My own Heroku for one Linux box.
projects.what: You upload an app or point Venvy at a git repo, and it runs, watches and publishes it. Every site on ringtwo.win runs on it, including this one.
story: It runs Python, Node, Bun, Deno, Go, Rust, PHP, Ruby, Java and static sites, and each app runs as its own Unix user, so one hacked app can't read the next one's files.

A deploy pulls, installs, builds, restarts and runs a health check. If the new release doesn't come up, Venvy puts the previous one back without anyone touching it. Each deploy is a release you can roll back to by hand later.

Venvy updates itself the same way. A release is checked against its signature and installed next to the running version, and the database is snapshotted. If the new version isn't healthy, the installer switches back.

It also has a browser terminal, live logs, cron jobs, CPU and memory alerts, backups to S3, WebDAV or scp, and a Cloudflare Tunnel that makes an app public with one click. The UI runs under a strict CSP with no inline script.
details: Uploads are chunked and resumable, so a big app survives a flaky connection.
Push webhooks from GitHub, GitLab, Gitea or Forgejo trigger a deploy.
The session cookie alone isn't enough: a per-origin key in localStorage stops hosted apps on the same host from riding the panel's session.

items: An app's terminal, running as that app's own Unix user.
Deploys are releases. Any of them can be rolled back to.

projects.why: My favourite. I've put more time into Venvy than into anything else, over a year, most of it before it went public on GitHub. It started because I wanted my own apps online without renting a platform, and grew into the thing all of them run on.

projects.name: Passable
projects.one: Drop in songs, get one continuous mix, built stem by stem.
projects.what: Every song is split into vocals, melody, drums and bass on the Mac. Then the set is ordered, and each transition is planned the way a DJ would plan it. Any of them can be opened and reshaped by hand.
story: Splitting runs on Core ML: HTDemucs v4 for drums, bass and melody, and Mel-Band RoFormer for the voice. The voice model gets 2.9 dB closer to the true vocal. After that come neural beat tracking, key detection, song structure and where each vocal line starts and ends.

Voices hand over between lines, on a breath. Line timing comes from on-device speech recognition, which gets the words wrong but the timing right. It's then snapped to a map of the singer's breaths, so nobody gets cut off mid-word.
A drummer's tempo drifts a percent or two from bar to bar. Each bar gets stretched to the average tempo, and the feel inside the bar stays. Songs whose tempo really changes get a grid bar by bar.

Requests during a set get downloaded, separated and mixed in after the current song without the music stopping. The whole set renders sample-exact to AAC or 24-bit WAV, or goes to the iPhone app over Wi-Fi.
details: The order is chosen to keep energy building toward the set's hardest song.
B's chorus or drop is placed to land as A leaves. There's never a chorus into a quiet intro.
One kick and one bass line at a time. The low end swaps on a single downbeat.

items: Transition 9 → 10 of a 59-song set, untouched. A's voice leaves at the end of its line, the melodies swap, and kick and bass change hands on one downbeat.
The set, ordered, with what each transition does.

projects.why: I wanted to know how hard it really is to automate what a DJ does. It turns out you need stem separation, beat tracking, key detection, and a detector for when a singer breathes.

projects.name: EAR Router
projects.one: The route planner for Meals on Wheels drivers in Vienna.
projects.what: It loads the day's tour, finds every door, orders the stops and predicts when the van gets to each one. Once loaded it works offline, and it has no third-party dependencies.
story: Addresses are looked up in Vienna's own building register first, with Nominatim as the fallback and a check that the result landed in the right district. The parser knows Stiege, Tür, garden-colony Parzelles and house numbers glued to the street name.

The stop order comes from my own OSRM server on the mini PC, with a public fallback. Arrival times come from the pace the driver actually kept that day, anchored to the last delivery. I backtested that model against 12 real tours.

The driver taps Geliefert at the door, in the stairwell, not where the van parked. So the app learns door time rather than parking time, and remembers which floor each customer lives on across every tour.

Before the van leaves the yard, a preflight checklist runs, while every failure is still cheap. On the road there's a next-stop screen, CarPlay, a read-only “Hey Siri, nächster Stopp”, and a hand-off to Apple Maps, Waze or Google Maps with the building's actual entrance.
details: A whole store backs up to one readable JSON file, because everything lives on one phone.
Stops behind the same front door are grouped together.
It ships by Xcode Run onto the driver's phone. A free developer profile lasts seven days, and the app keeps track of when it runs out.

items: The stop to drive to now.

projects.why: I'm doing my Zivildienst driving Essen auf Rädern, and I use this app on every tour. Most of the details below came from noticing what slowed me down on the road.

projects.name: Leeway
projects.one: A chartplotter that plans sailing routes around rocks, shallows and bad wind.
projects.what: It's a native iPhone chartplotter and passage planner with offline sea charts for the eastern Adriatic, from Istria to the Bay of Kotor. A Rust server I wrote builds and serves the charts.
story: Shortest finds the shortest path through water at least as deep as draft plus clearance. It stays clear of charted rocks, wrecks, obstructions, isolated-danger and cardinal marks, and bridges lower than the air draft plus a metre.

Fastest grows isochrones through the forecast wind using the boat's own polar, tacks and gybes where it pays, and runs the same safety checks. Every route is timed hourly with the finest available model (ICON-2I at 2.2 km, then ICON-EU, then global), plus waves and tidal streams. Bura gusts get flagged.

Underway it has a navigation bar with cross-track error, a Live Activity, man overboard, an anchor watch with a drag alarm, and an AIS collision alarm with CPA/TCPA limits. Alarms sound even with the phone on silent.

The charts come from open bathymetry, the Croatian Hydrographic Institute's open data and the national register of lights. A Rust / axum server on the same mini PC as this page turns them into vector tiles.
details: Light sectors are drawn with their characteristics, e.g. Fl(2)R.5s 12m 6M.
Tap anything on the chart for the object, its depth, the bearing and distance from the boat, and the next tide.
Polars can be imported from designers' tables or ORC certificates.

items: A weather-routed passage through the Kvarner.
The Kornati, with seamarks and soundings.

projects.why: I go boating, and I wanted a plotter that thinks about depth, wind and rocks the way I do when I plan a passage.

projects.name: garageDoor-pro
projects.one: A box in the car that opens the garage door when you leave and when you come home.
projects.what: There's no phone and no app involved. An ESP32-C3 and a GPS module press the button of a spare remote through one transistor. The box runs off the car's USB, so it boots with the ignition.
story: The underground garage has no GPS reception, so the board remembers in flash where it was parked. It knows at boot whether it's driving out or not.

There are two radii because GPS jitters at the edge. Arriving counts at 150 m and leaving at 300 m, so the state can't flap. A fix only counts with gnssFixOK, at most 50 m accuracy and at least 4 satellites.

The trip state machine is pure C, unit-tested on the host under AddressSanitizer and UBSan. The 4-layer board is generated from a Python netlist, so the schematic, layout, BOM and placement never disagree. There's also a perfboard version you can build in about an hour.
details: A captive-portal web panel sets home once, and the radii are configurable there.
OTA updates, LED status codes, and a 3D-printable case for the prototype.

items: garageDoor-pro v1.1, ESP32-C3-MINI-1 on four layers.

projects.why: Built for my own convenience: I wanted to stop fishing for the garage remote every time I drive in or out.

projects.name: dji-fcc-esp32
projects.one: A pocket dongle that replaces a phone app.
projects.what: You plug it into a DJI N1 remote. It patches the remote to FCC mode over USB, shows the result on an LED, and goes back to sleep.
story: The ESP32-S3 runs as a USB host and talks to the remote's CDC-ACM interface. Interfaces 0 and 1 are DJI-proprietary, and the serial one is 2.

The remote reports 512-byte bulk packets on a full-speed link, which Espressif's USB host stack rejects. So the project ships a patched copy of that stack, with the max-packet check relaxed and the TX FIFO sized to fit.

The battery-powered board is generated from one Python source and autorouted on 2 layers. It comes with Gerbers, BOM, placement and a STEP model. A Web Serial flasher on GitHub Pages flashes either build from Chrome, and CI redeploys it on every push.
details: The dev-board build is tested on a real remote. The custom board hasn't been assembled yet.
projects.why: Built for my own convenience: I didn't want to plug a phone into the drone remote and run an app every single time.

projects.name: ahm
projects.one: A crosshair overlay for Windows that uses no CPU while idle.
projects.what: It's one layered, click-through, topmost window holding a pre-rendered bitmap. It only redraws when a setting changes.
story: The overlay is plain Win32 in C. It lives in the tray and toggles with a global hotkey.
Settings are a separate WinUI 3 app that edits an ini file, which the overlay picks up live. The settings app exits when it's closed, so the XAML runtime never sits in memory.
Pushing a version tag builds the installer in GitHub Actions and publishes it.

intro: I'm Nikolaus, {age}, from Vienna. Most of what I build starts because I need it: a panel to run my own servers, a route planner for my Zivildienst tours, a chartplotter for the boat, and two little boards that save me a few annoying seconds every day. Sometimes it's just curiosity, like teaching a Mac to DJ.
